assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori's insight that atoms trapped in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength can be interrogated free of Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors turned atomic spectroscopy into a fractional-uncertainty regime near 1e-18. Fundamental precision of this kind lets one ask new questions (gravitational redshift across millimetres, variation of constants, a redefinition of the second). The underlying physics is a clean, well-understood use of atomic structure theory, which I can judge with confidence.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first demonstrated the Sr lattice clock; Ye brought it to the highest accuracy and stability and extended it to many-body and cavity-aided clocks. The two-person split is natural and well supported by the credited names. Other groups (Lemke/Ludlow-era NIST, Paris, PTB) contributed substantially, but the conceptual origin is clear.
assessment.maturity: Mature: many independent laboratories worldwide operate lattice clocks, agreement between them is routine, and the technology is entering international timekeeping. Recognition is timely and the field is not controversial.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wishes to treat optical clocks as a discovery of nature or as primarily an instrument and metrology advance.
How much of the credit belongs to the earlier frequency-comb work already recognized in 2005, and whether Ye's comb work overlaps with that prize.
I rely on recollection for details of the earliest independent demonstrations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Loading ultracold atoms into optical lattices gave a controllable, tunable realisation of Hubbard models, with the observation of the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes. This lets us answer questions about many-body quantum mechanics directly in the laboratory and is a clear case of a tool that revealed physics in an unexpectedly controlled way.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and collaborators) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner (with Hänsch and Bloch) observed the Mott transition; Bloch built the field, including quantum gas microscopy and many-body dynamics. Esslinger's fermionic Hubbard work is also decisive and its omission from a triple is a real allocation problem. Zoller also appears under B038, which would conflict in practice.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by many groups for more than two decades and increasingly moving to quantum simulation of open questions. Recognition would be timely, though 2001 and 2012 prizes already covered the neighbouring cold-atom fields.
uncertainties: Allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller is genuinely contested.
The overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems may argue against.
Whether the quantum-simulation payoff is yet a settled discovery or still maturing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions defined a concrete physical architecture for quantum computation, and the ion experiments that followed showed entangling gates, teleportation and error-corrected operations with high fidelity. This is quantum mechanics put under demanding, precise control, and continues the direction of the 2012 and 2025 prizes.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive theory proposal (1995); Blatt built the leading experimental realisation, though Wineland (already a laureate) and Monroe also made decisive experimental contributions. The triple is plausible but leaves out Monroe and the credited names do not include him; Zoller overlaps with B050.
assessment.maturity: The ion-trap platform is confirmed by several independent laboratories and companies. The broader claim of useful quantum computing is not mature, but the physical foundation is.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and the possibility that the committee wants to wait on a more decisive quantum-computing milestone.
Credit split among theory proposers and experimental groups, and with Zoller appearing in two candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling a mechanical object to its quantum ground state, entangling and squeezing macroscopic motion, and quantum-limited readout through radiation pressure speak directly to where the boundary between quantum and everyday mechanical behaviour lies. That is the kind of fundamental question I care about most, and it follows naturally from last year's prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and collaborators demonstrated ground-state cooling of a mechanical resonator; Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer developed cavity optomechanics and sideband cooling in the optical domain. The three-way split looks workable, though other groups (Teufel, Lehnert, Harris, Painter) made comparably decisive demonstrations, and I cannot be sure about relative priority.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature as a field with many independent groups, but the most striking quantum-regime results are only about a decade old, and the interpretation of some entanglement experiments is still being refined.
uncertainties: Competing claims from Teufel, Lehnert, Painter, Harris and others for the key demonstrations.
The overlap with the 2025 prize may make the committee reluctant to award circuit-adjacent macroscopic quantum work again so soon.
Whether this is a single discovery or an assembly of related advances.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gives inertial and gravitational measurements at extraordinary precision (gravimetry, rotation, determination of constants, tests of the equivalence principle). It is quantum mechanics used as a precision tool, and the principle is simple and convincing.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard demonstrated atom interferometry with gratings and developed fundamental measurements; Kasevich realised the light-pulse sensors that reach high precision; Bordé laid the theoretical basis for atom interferometry with light pulses. Chu's contributions, already honoured in 1997 for laser cooling, are not among the credited names, and the credit among these three seems fair but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed and used in many laboratories, with commercial gravimeters in the field. Large-scale fundamental-physics applications are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with 1997 and 2001 prizes in the same community.
Whether the fundamental discovery content is greater than the instrumental content.
Attribution among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and others such as Chu and Mlynek is not clearly settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision (three-step) picture and its quantum formulation explain high harmonic generation and underlie attosecond science. I know this field closely, and I judge the model to be a decisive and original understanding of why the harmonic plateau exists, but much of the field was already recognised by the 2023 prize.
assessment.attribution: Corkum and the Schafer/Kulander group introduced the semiclassical recollision picture in 1993 and Lewenstein with L'Huillier and co-workers gave the quantum theory in 1994; the credit among them is plausible but the Lewenstein paper also had L'Huillier as co-author, who is already a laureate. I should be careful because of my close collaboration with L'Huillier.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and confirmed across many laboratories, but the issue is whether it is timely given the 2023 award.
uncertainties: Whether the 2023 prize leaves room for a theoretical complement three years later.
Attribution between Corkum, Schafer, Kulander, Lewenstein and L'Huillier.
My own proximity to this community means I should discount my enthusiasm.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states of light reduce quantum noise below the vacuum level and are now used in gravitational-wave detectors to extend their reach. The idea is conceptually beautiful and the application is directly visible in observatories.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezing in interferometers; Kimble and co-workers (and Slusher's group, not listed) first demonstrated squeezed light; Mavalvala led the implementation in LIGO. Roman Schnabel's GEO600 work is also decisive. The allocation is unclear because origin, demonstration and application sit with different people.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense of squeezed light in LIGO and Virgo, but the prize overlap with the 2017 gravitational-wave prize and the 1989 and 2012 prizes is a concern.
uncertainties: Attribution is difficult because the first experimental squeezing involved Slusher and others not credited.
Overlap with the 2017 LIGO prize.
Whether the committee sees this as a discovery or an enabling technique.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The thorium-229 isomer has an extraordinarily low nuclear excitation energy that can be reached with a laser, giving a nuclear clock that links atomic and nuclear physics and gives sensitivity to variations of fundamental constants. The 2024 laser excitation was striking and interesting, and I am drawn to it because it is unexpected and fundamental.
assessment.attribution: Peik proposed the nuclear clock concept; Schumm's and other groups worked on the isomer and its excitation; Ye's group performed the frequency-comb laser spectroscopy in a crystal. The attribution is plausible but experimental credit was shared among several collaborations (including Tokyo and PTB-led groups) and cannot be fully captured by three names.
assessment.maturity: Premature: the key result is only about two years old, the clock itself has not been operated as a clock and independent confirmations, though promising, are few.
uncertainties: The decisive experiments are very recent and the interpretation of the isomer properties is still developing.
Credit is spread over several teams.
I am uncertain of the exact details of the most recent measurements.
